new_statements.quote: STRESS $A "The stress group consists of a sequence of from one to four syllables with one primary stress. Stress is phonemic. It usually occurs on the penultimate syllable." The only, exception is certain words that end in particular vowel sequences, (p. 102) [...] LONG VOWELS $A "Each long vowel is interpreted as two like phonemes because (1) there are frequent vowel clusters in the language, and (2) this interpretation best coincides with the predominant stress pattern." (p. 105) [...] Priest interprets the vocalic segments [i] and [u] as consonantal /yod/ and /w/ when they occur unstressed, intervocalically within a word or word initially before a vowel. "This interpretation results in the fewest possible exceptions to the predominant stress pattern." (p. 105)

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog's StressTyp2 record (penultimate: penultimate stress). Adds the domain (stress group of 1-4 syllables, one primary stress), the phonemic status, the exception class (words ending in particular vowel sequences), and the syllable-count conventions (long vowel = two syllables; unstressed i/u = glides) that make the penult rule hold. Quote is the scanned text of the SPA page; 'The only, exception' has a stray scanned comma. This is a secondary source quoting Priest 1968 (the SIL record for which is held by the project from yesterday; the article itself is de Gruyter DOI 10.1515/ling.1968.6.41.102, paywalled).
new_statements.rule_in_words: One primary stress per stress group of one to four syllables; stress is phonemic but falls on the penultimate syllable in the default case. The only exceptions are certain words ending in particular vowel sequences. Long vowels count as two syllables (VV), and unstressed prevocalic/intervocalic i, u are treated as glides, both analyses chosen so that the penultimate pattern has the fewest exceptions.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned (only one primary stress per stress group).
new_statements.exceptions: Certain words that end in particular vowel sequences (Priest 1968 p. 102, as summarised by SPA); Priest calls stress phonemic, so a residual lexical component exists.
new_statements.identity_note: The SPA entry (and Priest 1968 behind it) describes the Sirionó of eastern Bolivia between the Mamoré and Blanco rivers (Beni), from Priest's fieldwork 1957-1965; no sub-dialect is named. Both listed Priest works are by the same fieldworker on the same variety.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: all three deciding sentences found verbatim in the Gasparini 2012 PDF we hold at printed pp. 46 and 97 (PDF p. 52 verified with extracted text on that page). (2) Deciding source is a 2012 fieldwork-based phonology sketch (M2 thesis, 136 pp, with spectrographic evidence) that explicitly settles the only live disagreement in the literature (penultimate syllable vs penultimate mora) and reviews Priest 1968, Firestone 1963, Crowhurst 2000 and Dahl. Three further held primaries independently state penult: Priest 1980 §1 (phonemic but 'por lo general' penult, exceptions = some words in final Vi/Vɨ sequences), Priest & Priest 1967 §5.1.1 (clitic stress group, penult stressed), Gasparini & Dicarere 2015 dictionary p. 9.
